source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-most prompting enables complex reasoning (full text, GSM8K and DROP tables)
finding: Full-text check of the GSM8K and DROP results. The table says chain-of-thought 60.87; the prose says 60.97. The table is the source number, so the inconsistency is the paper's own typo. Gain is largest on problems needing 5 or more steps and on DROP, which splits easily.
numbers: GSM8K (code-davinci-002): CoT 60.87, least-to-most 62.39 (+1.52). By steps: 2 steps 76.68 CoT vs 74.53 LtM (CoT better); 3 steps 67.29 vs 68.91; 4 steps 59.39 vs 59.73; 5+ steps 39.07 vs 45.23. DROP numerical: non-football 74.77 vs 82.45; football 59.56 vs 73.42. Zero-shot GSM8K 16.38, standard prompting 17.06.
quote: least-to-most prompting only slightly improves chain-of-thought prompting: from 60.97% to 62.39%
limits: One model (code-davinci-002), few-shot exemplars. Decomposition hurt slightly on 2-step problems. Authors say nearly all failures are fixed by a hand-made decomposition, so the weak point is generating the decomposition, not solving subparts.
agent_relevance: Decompose only when a task has many steps or splits easily; for short problems it can cost accuracy. Use 60.87 as the CoT baseline.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Mollick & Shapiro (2025) Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
finding: Tested explicit 'think step by step' on GPQA Diamond. For non-reasoning models it raised the average a little but made some easy questions fail. For dedicated reasoning models it gave almost nothing and cost 20-80% more time. CoT prompt variants, including 'First, decompose the problem', made negligible differences (GPT-4o, 100 samples per question).
numbers: 198 questions x 25 trials = 4,950 runs per prompt per model. Non-reasoning, CoT vs direct, average rating: Gemini Flash 2.0 RD +0.135, Sonnet 3.5 +0.117, GPT-4o-mini +0.044 (ns, p=.067). 100%-correct metric: Sonnet 3.5 +0.101, GPT-4o +0.01 (ns), Gemini Flash 2.0 -0.131, Gemini Pro 1.5 -0.172. Versus no-prompt default: Flash 2.0 +0.062, GPT-4o +0.069, Sonnet 3.5 -0.019 (ns), GPT-4o-mini +0.004 (ns). Reasoning models CoT vs direct: o3-mini +0.029 (p=.024), o4-mini +0.031 (p=.003), Gemini Flash 2.5 -0.033 (p=.005). CoT time: +35-600% non-reasoning, +20-80% reasoning.
quote: for dedicated reasoning models, the added benefits of explicit CoT prompting appear negligible
limits: One benchmark (multiple-choice, graduate science), simple CoT, temperature 0, models from 2024 to early 2025. Not a test of structured decomposition with fed-forward answers.
agent_relevance: Expertise-reversal echo for models: a generic step-by-step scaffold has near-zero value on reasoning-mode models and costs time. Gate the scaffold on model type, and measure at equal tokens.

source: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Zero-shot Can Be Stronger than Few-shot (arXiv 2506.14641 v3, Jan 2026)
finding: For strong Qwen2.5 models on GSM8K and MATH, adding worked CoT exemplars did not beat zero-shot CoT. Exemplars mainly fixed output format. Even exemplars written by Qwen2.5-Max or DeepSeek-R1 did not help. Models seemed to ignore the exemplars and follow the instruction.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B and 72B, GSM8K and MATH; 8-shot (random, top-k, fast-votek), R1-written 4-shot and Qwen-max 8-shot vs zero-shot. Exact accuracies are in plots that were not read as numbers. A noise-injection ablation on exemplars was also run.
quote: adding traditional CoT exemplars does not improve reasoning performance compared to Zero-Shot CoT
limits: Instruction-tuned Qwen models only, math only. Conclusions read in the text; per-cell numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Worked-example scaffolds add tokens without gain for strong models that already know the procedure. Supports an off-switch for exemplar scaffolds.

source: Innate Reasoning is Not Enough: In-Context Learning Enhances Reasoning Large Language Models with Less Overthinking (arXiv 2503.19602)
finding: Opposite direction to d02 and d03: for R1-distilled and similar reasoning models (1.5B-32B), CoT prompting still helped in most cases on math, and one-shot beat few-shot. Large models gained mainly on hard problems; small models mainly on easy ones. Exemplars cut excessive reflection.
numbers: CoT (zero- or few-shot) improved accuracy in 72% of cases in Table 1. Case study: R1-32B thinking tokens fell from 1,088 (15 steps) to 420 (12 steps), -61.4%, under few-shot CoT. Abstract: excessive reflections reduced by about 90% in some cases.
quote: CoT prompting significantly enhances RLLMs' performance in most scenarios
limits: Math only, open distilled models. Disagrees with DeepSeek-R1's own advice (zero-shot best). The gain may partly be token saving, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Scaffold effect on strong reasoning models depends on task difficulty and model size, so an on/off test by model needs a difficulty axis too.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning (Limitations section)
finding: The developers report that R1 is sensitive to prompts and that few-shot prompting consistently lowers its performance. They recommend describing the problem directly and the output format, zero-shot.
numbers: No number in the passage read. Page read to character 100,000 of about 142,000.
quote: it is sensitive to prompts. Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
limits: Developer statement, not a controlled study. Conflicts with d04.
agent_relevance: For reasoning-mode models, default to the lean prompt and add scaffold only when a test shows a gain.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Bears on gap 6 (self-verification of hints and plans). Without an oracle label, asking the model to review and fix its answer did not help and often hurt. The earlier gains came from oracle labels telling the model when it was wrong. Self-consistency beat multi-agent debate at equal numbers of responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 (round 1) -> 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 95.5. Equal responses on GSM8K: self-consistency with 3 responses 82.5 vs multi-agent debate round 1 76.7; self-consistency 6 responses 85.3 vs debate round 2 83.2; 9 responses 88.2 vs 83.0.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023), tasks with fixed answers. Newer reasoning models trained for self-checking were not tested.
agent_relevance: A self-written hint or plan cannot be trusted just because the same model re-reads it. Use an independent check: an executable test, a vote over fresh samples, or a ground-truth step. Voting costs N times the tokens.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Pay for Hints, Not Answers: LLM Shepherding for Cost-Efficient Inference
finding: Inference-time hint length test (gap 4). A strong model writes only the first part of an answer (a prefix hint) and a small model finishes it. Accuracy broadly rises with hint length from the smallest hints, but not smoothly. Most items need no hint at all.
numbers: Llama-3.2-3B with Llama-3.3-70B hints, GSM8K, steps of 10% up to 90%; large-model accuracy 98.0%. Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K accuracy by hint share 0 to 90%: 84.8, 87.8, 86.2, 89.2, 89.8, 91.2, 93.3, 94.2, 94.8, 95.2 (+10.4). The 1B/3B/8B models recover about 60%/81%/79% of the gap to the big model. The 8B passes 89% at a 30% hint; the 3B needs 70%. On GSM8K 80.6% of queries need no hint; the rest need 10-90%. A learned hint-size predictor cut cost 33-65% vs big-model-only and up to 4x vs routing and cascading. HumanEval with a GSM8K-trained policy: 77.4% accuracy, 44% cost cut. HumanEval accuracy dips at 10%, 30% and 60% hints.
limits: Solution-prefix hints only (not knowledge or plan hints), no comparison with other hint types, small-model and large-model pairs, per-token cost model.
agent_relevance: A measured dose curve for prefix hints: broadly rising, and the weakest model exploits hints least. Hint length can be set per item by a cheap predictor. The 50% rule from RL training is not tested here.

source: HintMR authors (2026) HintMR: Eliciting Stronger Mathematical Reasoning in Small Language Models
finding: Step-by-step hints at inference time. A stronger model writes a hint for the next step from the solver's partial work, with rules that hints must not reveal the answer or future steps. Hints helped small reasoning models. A small hint writer distilled from the big one gave much of the gain.
numbers: MATH-500 subset of 74 problems: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct 75.68% (56/74) with no hint, 85.14% (63/74) with LLM hints; Phi-4-mini-reasoning 56.76% -> 77.03% with LLM hints and 74.32% with SLM hints; R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 85.14% with SLM hints. NuminaMath: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct 78.67% with LLM hints (+32.00). AIME-2024: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 68.97% (+48.28) with LLM hints; R1-Distill-Llama-8B 0.00 -> 44.83%. AIME-2025 gains smaller. The paper says SLM hints never lowered accuracy.
limits: Small test sets (74 problems; AIME has 30), hint writer trained on the same domain, token cost of the hint loop not extracted.
agent_relevance: Next-step hints that carry no answer lift small models a lot, and the gain does not vanish on distilled long-CoT models here, unlike the +5.9% in Scaf-GRPO. Mixed evidence on expertise reversal.

source: Hou et al. (2026) Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
finding: Within-subject test of contingent LLM support (CoMeT: help rises after failure at a decision point, fades after take-up) against an answer-giving assistant (A) and a question-only tutor (B) on three Python tasks. Measured demand, load, delegation and frustration. Did NOT measure later unaided learning.
numbers: 131 adults completed all three tasks (162 began), 393 sessions, six tutor orders (Williams square). Perceived load 3.36/3.30/3.29 and germane load 3.85/3.74/3.78 across tutors, equivalent by TOST. Effort: CoMeT above assistant by +0.46 (Holm p<.001). Build requests in 50.4% of CoMeT sessions, 51.1% assistant, 23.7% question-only. Tutor-written artifact delivered: CoMeT 48.1%, assistant 23.7%, question-only 9.2%. Full answer given away in 1 of 16 sessions for CoMeT vs 1 of 6 for question-only (abstract). Abstract: frustrated learners less than question-only tutor.
limits: Adult learners, one short session, self-report plus log, no delayed unaided test, no equal-token comparison. Tutors differ in what they may say, so not a pure test of contingency.
agent_relevance: The only direct LLM contingent-vs-fixed comparison found. It supports contingent rules for experience and for an escape (fewer full answers than answer-giving, less frustration than question-only), not for later learning. Closes gap 2 only in part.

source: Cohn et al. (2026) Evidence-Decision-Feedback: Theory-Driven Adaptive Scaffolding for LLM Agents
finding: Framework (Copa peer agent) with evidence inference, decision, feedback. In a high school class it logged feedback aligned to demonstrated mastery and fading of scaffolds, with no sign of overreliance.
numbers: Authentic classroom study; no control arm and no delayed unaided test in the text read. The paper cites Kosmyna et al.: 83% of students using ChatGPT while writing could not quote their own work.
limits: No comparison of adaptive vs fixed support, so it shows that fading can be logged, not that it helps.
agent_relevance: Same status as K20: fading is implementable but its outcome benefit is untested.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne & Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning (Scientific Reports 15:17458), full text
finding: Gap 8. The paper says a system prompt alone could not reliably scaffold multi-part problems, because the tutor sometimes discussed parts out of sequence. So the platform guided students through each part in code. The paper gives no ablation of prompt-only vs code-enforced order and no token cost.
numbers: Linear regression effect 0.63 SD on post-test (p<10^-8), judged an underestimate from ceiling; quantile regression range 0.73 to 1.3 SD. Median AI time on task 49 min vs 60 min assumed in class; 70% of AI students under 60 min. Time on task did not correlate with post-test. 83% said AI explanations were as good as or better than the instructor's. Step-by-step worked solutions were put in the prompt to limit errors.
quote: a system prompt could not reliably provide enough structure to scaffold problems with multiple parts
limits: One course, one site, crossover over two lessons, short-term test. The sequencing claim is an experience report, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Supports code-enforced step order only as a designer's observation. Gap 8 stays open for a measured test.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (PNAS), page text via PMC
finding: Gap 7. Page text read through a fetch tool (summary, not verbatim). Unrestricted ChatGPT-style help raised practice scores but cut later unaided exam scores. A tutor with teacher-written solutions and hint-not-answer rules removed the harm but did not produce a gain on the unaided exam.
numbers: Nearly 1,000 high school students, about 50 classes, four 90-minute sessions in Turkey. Practice: GPT Base +48%, GPT Tutor +127% vs control. Unaided exam: GPT Base -17%; GPT Tutor -0.004 on a 0-1 scale (not significant). GPT Base was right only 51% of the time (42% of its errors logical, 8% arithmetic). GPT Base students did not think they learned less; GPT Tutor students thought they did better.
limits: Humans learning, not a model with memory. One school, one subject, short. Guardrails removed harm but added no benefit, so the withholding rule is protective, not proven helpful.
agent_relevance: Reason to keep an answer-withholding rule for any memory the agent writes for itself, but expect no gain. No test yet of an agent copying answers into memory.

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving (second open attempt)
finding: Could not open the paper: the publisher link returned a web page, not the PDF, and the metadata services were rate limited. Gap 10 for the 1976 numbers remains open.

finding: Could not open the full text (the university file link returned a web page, not a PDF; the DOI metadata lookup failed). The 77% vs 23% split stays unverified.

source: SEELE authors (2025) Staying in the Sweet Spot: Responsive Reasoning Evolution via Capability-Adaptive Hint Scaffolding
finding: SEELE is RL training, not prompting. It derives that learning efficiency peaks when rollout accuracy is near 50%, and adjusts hint length per problem to stay there. So the 50%-success rule is a training-time result about gradient signal, not a prompting result.
numbers: Average +11.8 points over GRPO and +10.5 over SFT on in-domain math (Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3B); above the best baseline by 1.7% (3B) and 3.8% (1.5B). The Item Response Theory fit needs about 3 samples per problem; 4 are enough; by round 3-4 accuracy is near the 50% target.
limits: Training-time. The 50% argument concerns gradient signal for RL, which a frozen model with a prompt does not have. For prompting, the only dose curve found is d07.
agent_relevance: Do not copy the 50% rule to prompts as is. At inference, test hint length against measured first-try success and token cost instead.
